Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents

SilverFox Targets Japanese Manufacturer with 3-Driver BYOVD Chain and ValleyRAT

The Hacker News
2026-07-30 15 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Chinese cybercrime group known as Silver Fox has been observed using new drivers as part of bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) attacks targeting a Japanese organization in the industrial manufacturing sector to ultimately deliver ValleyRAT (aka Winos 4.0) for persistent remote access. "In this campaign, the group combines new vulnerable-driver abuse, newly observed abuse of legitimate

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Downloader retrieval from SilverFox Tencent COS bucket · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SilverFox multi-driver BYOVD payload dropped (BootRepair/EnPortv/wsftprm/amsdk .sys) · [LLM] BYOVD driver service registration for SilverFox vulnerable drivers · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — SilverFox Targets Japanese Manufacturer with 3-Driver BYOVD Chain and ValleyRAT
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Zeon-signed ConvertToPDF.exe / PDFDirect.exe side-loading PDFCORE8.dll (SilverFox) · [LLM] SilverFox watchdog persistence: scheduled task launching a batch loader · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ValleyRAT C2 / shellcode fetch to 43.128.26.132 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Zeon-signed ConvertToPDF.exe / PDFDirect.exe side-loading PDFCORE8.dll (SilverFox) AIInstallation High
Hunts the SilverFox DLL side-load where the legitimate Zeon Corporation binaries ConvertToPDF.exe or PDFDirect.exe load the malicious PDFCORE8.dll that embeds the three-driver BYOVD framework and the ValleyRAT loader. Article-specific because both the host binary names and the sideloaded DLL name are named IOCs, not a generic sideloading template. Rationale: Anchors on three named IOCs from the article — the two Zeon-signed host binaries (ConvertToPDF.exe / PDFDirect.exe) and the malicious PDFCORE8.dll — a combination that has no legitimate occurrence. Cross-checked against Cato and SC Media which both name these binaries and Zeon Corporation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/silver-fox-group-uses-new-drivers-in-byovd-attacks-against-japanese-manufacturer • https://securityaffairs.com/196347/apt/silverfox-targets-japanese-manufacturer-with-advanced-valleyrat-campaign.html
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Zeon Corporation PDF-conversion product installed under Program Files legitimately loading its own PDFCORE8.dll (rare; path filter in SPL reduces this)
  • Internal software-packaging/SCCM staging of the Zeon installer in a temp directory during deployment
  • Security-researcher / malware-analysis sandbox detonating the sample on a monitored host
  • Portable/no-install PDF tool run from Downloads by a power user
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full folder of ConvertToPDF.exe/PDFDirect.exe and confirm PDFCORE8.dll is co-located and unsigned/mismatched-signer; check DeviceFileEvents for who wrote the ZIP/DLL and its FileOriginUrl. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the writing process tree, and quarantine PDFCORE8.dll plus any .sys files dropped alongside it. 3) Hunt: search the estate for the same PDFCORE8.dll SHA256, the four BYOVD driver names, and connections to 43.128.26.132 to scope lateral spread.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "PDFCORE8.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ConvertToPDF.exe","PDFDirect.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoadedDll = FileName, DllPath = FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "PDFCORE8.dll" or (ActingProcessName has_any ("ConvertToPDF.exe","PDFDirect.exe") and TargetFileName endswith ".dll")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SilverFox DLL Side-Load PDFCORE8.dll via ConvertToPDF/PDFDirect
id: 8f1c2a4e-7b3d-4e2a-9c11-6a2f0d9e1b34
description: Legitimate Zeon Corporation binaries ConvertToPDF.exe or PDFDirect.exe loading the malicious PDFCORE8.dll used by SilverFox to stage a three-driver BYOVD chain and ValleyRAT.
references:
  - https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/silverfox-targets-japanese-manufacturer.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\ConvertToPDF.exe'
      - '\PDFDirect.exe'
    ImageLoaded|endswith: '\PDFCORE8.dll'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 @Image:(*\ConvertToPDF.exe OR *\converttopdf.exe OR *\PDFDirect.exe OR *\pdfdirect.exe) @ImageLoaded:(*\PDFCORE8.dll OR *\pdfcore8.dll)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(ConvertToPDF|PDFDirect)\.exe$/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/\\Program Files( \(x86\))?\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("ConvertToPDF.exe","PDFDirect.exe")) AND NOT (Processes.process_path IN ("*\\Program Files\\*","*\\Program Files (x86)\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("ConvertToPDF.exe","PDFDirect.exe")) AND NOT (Processes.process_path IN ("*\\Program Files\\*","*\\Program Files (x86)\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
SilverFox multi-driver BYOVD payload dropped (BootRepair/EnPortv/wsftprm/amsdk .sys) AIExploitation High
Detects the write of the SilverFox BYOVD driver set — BootRepair.sys, EnPortv.sys, wsftprm.sys and amsdk.sys — that PDFCORE8.dll embeds and deploys as a plug-and-play kernel-evasion framework. Surfaces the count of distinct driver files per host/process so analysts can see the '2+ / three-driver' loading sequence the article describes. Rationale: Uses the four exact driver filenames named across Cato (BootRepair.sys/EnPortv.sys — newly observed) and Check Point (amsdk.sys/CVE-2023-52271, wsftprm.sys). These names co-occurring, especially 2+ from one dropping process, is unique to this BYOVD framework. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/silver-fox-apt-vulnerable-drivers/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/silver-fox-exploits-microsoft-signed.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1543.003 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate FTP/router product genuinely installing wsftprm.sys under System32\drivers via its MSI (single driver, signed installer parent)
  • Endpoint vendor packaging amsdk.sys during a supported WatchDog/Zemana AV install
  • Driver-signing test lab or WHQL submission workflow writing .sys files to a staging path
  • Backup/imaging tool restoring a drivers folder that already contained one of these files
Suppression filter
| where not (DriverCount == 1 and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe") and Drivers has "wsftprm.sys")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which of the four drivers landed, the writing process (should trace back to PDFCORE8.dll / the downloader), and whether a matching \CurrentControlSet\Services entry was created. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop and delete the driver service, and quarantine the .sys files and their dropper; assume kernel-level EDR tampering occurred. 3) Hunt: check for security-tool process terminations around the drop time, NTDLL unhooking artifacts, and the same driver SHA256s or ConvertToPDF/PDFDirect binaries on other hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("BootRepair.sys","EnPortv.sys","wsftprm.sys","amsdk.sys")
| summarize DriverCount = dcount(FileName), Drivers = make_set(FileName), Paths = make_set(FolderPath), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), SHA256s = make_set(SHA256) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("BootRepair.sys","EnPortv.sys","wsftprm.sys","amsdk.sys")
| summarize DriverCount = dcount(TargetFileName), Drivers = make_set(TargetFileName), Paths = make_set(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc

BYOVD driver service registration for SilverFox vulnerable drivers AIExploitation High
Detects creation/modification of a Windows kernel-driver service under HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services for the SilverFox driver names, which is how the loader registers each vulnerable .sys before opening a device handle to it. Complements the file-drop UC by catching the service-installation half of the BYOVD chain. Rationale: Service key names under CurrentControlSet\Services matching the four BYOVD driver names is a direct, low-noise indicator of driver registration for this campaign; the ImagePath value data will point at the dropped .sys for confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/silver-fox-apt-vulnerable-drivers/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate install of the WatchDog/Zemana anti-malware product registering the amsdk service
  • A genuine FTP router utility registering wsftprm as a driver service
  • Golden-image build pipeline pre-registering vendor driver services
  • Vendor uninstall routine rewriting the same service key during cleanup
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryKey has "amsdk" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","services.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("system","trustedinstaller"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the ImagePath/RegistryValueData to confirm it references a .sys in a suspicious path and correlate the writing process with the PDFCORE8.dll chain. 2) Contain: delete the service, prevent driver load (WDAC/driver blocklist), and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the InitiatingProcess to find the loader and dropped drivers, and sweep the fleet for the same service names.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"CurrentControlSet\Services"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("BootRepair","EnPortv","wsftprm","amsdk")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has "CurrentControlSet\\Services"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("BootRepair","EnPortv","wsftprm","amsdk")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ValleyRAT C2 / shellcode fetch to 43.128.26.132 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host connecting to the SilverFox C2 server 43.128.26.132, which the loader contacts to fetch shellcode that it thread-context-hijacks into a new svchost.exe — the ValleyRAT (Winos 4.0) command-and-control channel. Any outbound connection to this IP is high-confidence, and svchost.exe as the initiating process makes it near-certain. Rationale: 43.128.26.132 is the exact C2 IP named in the article for shellcode retrieval; a static IOC with no legitimate business use. svchost.exe as InitiatingProcess (from the thread-context-hijack injection) is a decisive escalator when present. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/silverfox-targets-japanese-manufacturer.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1095 T1055.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • This is a Tencent-range IP that could be reassigned to a benign tenant months later (validate against first-seen date of the campaign)
  • A researcher intentionally connecting to the IOC from a sandbox for analysis
  • Threat-intel scanner or connectivity-check tooling probing the IP
  • Shared-hosting reuse where a legitimate service later occupies the same address
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess — svchost.exe with an unusual parent or a non-service svchost strongly indicates the injected ValleyRAT stage; capture the process tree and loaded modules. 2) Contain: block 43.128.26.132 at the egress/firewall, isolate the host, and suspend the injected svchost. 3) Hunt: sweep for the PDFCORE8.dll sideload, the four BYOVD drivers, the watchdog scheduled task, and any other hosts beaconing to the same IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "43.128.26.132"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "43.128.26.132"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Downloader retrieval from SilverFox Tencent COS bucket AIDelivery High
Detects hosts resolving/connecting to the attacker-controlled Tencent Cloud Object Storage bucket hrefbfdhfhgre-1422102728.cos.ap-hongkong.myqcloud.com, from which the ZIP's downloader executable pulls the DLL-side-loading components. Targets the specific bucket hostname rather than the shared myqcloud.com parent so it stays high-fidelity. Rationale: The full bucket hostname is a pre-extracted IOC unique to this campaign; matching the whole FQDN (not the shared myqcloud.com suffix) keeps false positives near zero while still catching the downloader's staging fetch. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/silverfox-targets-japanese-manufacturer.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researcher or crawler resolving the IOC domain for analysis/enrichment
  • DNS sinkhole or passive-DNS collector logging the lookup without a real host infection
  • Proxy/secure-web-gateway pre-resolving the URL during inline inspection of a quarantined sample
  • Bucket later deleted and the label reused by benign Tencent COS content
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — a non-browser downloader (e.g. an exe from a ZIP in Downloads/Temp) fetching from this bucket is the delivery stage; capture the downloaded artifacts. 2) Contain: block the FQDN and its resolved IPs at egress, isolate the host, and quarantine the ZIP/downloader. 3) Hunt: look for subsequent PDFCORE8.dll sideload, BYOVD driver drops, and 43.128.26.132 beacons on the same and neighbouring hosts.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "hrefbfdhfhgre-1422102728.cos.ap-hongkong.myqcloud.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SilverFox watchdog persistence: scheduled task launching a batch loader AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the external watchdog component — a batch script registered as a scheduled task that relaunches the SilverFox loader if it is terminated. Focuses on schtasks.exe /create actions that install a .bat task and are spawned from the loader chain, part of the article's dual-watchdog recovery design. Rationale: The article explicitly describes an external watchdog batch script persisted via a scheduled task; tying schtasks /create + .bat to the loader parents (ConvertToPDF/PDFDirect and injected svchost) keeps this campaign-scoped rather than a generic scheduled-task rule. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196347/apt/silverfox-targets-japanese-manufacturer-with-advanced-valleyrat-campaign.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin/GPO scripts registering a maintenance .bat scheduled task via cmd.exe
  • Software installers that create a batch-driven updater task
  • Backup or logon scripts wrapped in .bat and scheduled by IT
  • RMM tooling deploying batch-based scheduled tasks fleet-wide
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("system","network service","local service")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the /tr target of the scheduled task and open the referenced .bat — SilverFox's watchdog will reference the loader (PDFCORE8/ConvertToPDF chain) or a payload in AppData/Temp. 2) Contain: delete the scheduled task and the .bat, isolate the host, and remember to also kill the loader and injected svchost so the dual-watchdog cannot restore either stage. 3) Hunt: enumerate all scheduled tasks and Run keys pointing at batch/loader files, and correlate with the BYOVD drivers and 43.128.26.132 to confirm the intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ProcessCommandLine has ".bat"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ConvertToPDF.exe","PDFDirect.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","svchost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "/create" and TargetProcessCommandLine has ".bat"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ConvertToPDF.exe","PDFDirect.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","svchost.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Egress to code.newcli.com anti-attribution AI proxy (knaithe/KnYuan) AICommand & Control High
Hunts host DNS/connections to code.newcli.com, the third-party proxy this actor routed Claude Code (/ultra) and Codex (/codex/v1) through to strip attribution. Any internal host resolving this domain indicates the actor's Western-LLM tooling running in your estate. Rationale: code.newcli.com is a hard IOC named in Table 1 (proxy paths /ultra and /codex/v1) and independently reported by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News; it has no legitimate enterprise use, making DNS resolution a near-zero-FP signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-uses-deepseek-ai-to-autonomously-attack-vulnerable-servers/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chinese-hacker-commands-deepseek-via.html
ATT&CKT1090 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher on the team intentionally studying this campaign's IOCs in a sandbox
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively fetching the domain to confirm sinkhole status
  • DNS logging that captures passive-DNS mirror traffic rather than a real host resolution
  • Typosquat collision where an unrelated *.newcli.com subdomain is legitimately registered
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\SecurityTools\\", "\\ThreatIntel\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess and user on the resolving host; confirm whether an AI coding CLI (claude, codex, node) or an unexpected binary generated the lookup. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block newcli.com at the resolver/proxy, and preserve ~/.claude, ~/.codex and shell history for the account. 3) Hunt: pivot the same host/user to UC 'DeepSeek/Qwen direct API egress' and to the anti-attribution config-string UC to establish full tooling footprint.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "newcli.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "newcli.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI coding-tool anti-attribution / auto-approve config strings AIInstallation Medium
Hunts process command lines that set the exact anti-attribution and safety-bypass options this actor used: CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1, --dangerously-skip-permissions, disable_response_storage=true, and approvalMode yolo. These indicate an AI agent deliberately configured to bypass logging and human approval. Rationale: Every string is quoted verbatim from Table 1 (CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER:"0", disable_response_storage=true, dangerously-skip-permissions:true, approvalMode:"yolo"); together they describe an agent explicitly stripped of logging/approval and rarely co-occur in benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chinese-hacker-commands-deepseek-via.html
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sanctioned developer running Claude Code with --dangerously-skip-permissions inside a disposable dev container
  • Internal red team replaying this exact TTP during an authorized exercise
  • CI/CD pipeline that sets approvalMode yolo for a headless code-generation job
  • Documentation or IaC files containing these keys read into a process command line (grep/cat of a settings file)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["approved-ai-dev-01","approved-ai-dev-02"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the account is a real developer vs. service/unexpected user, and whether the host is a sanctioned AI-dev workstation; read the surrounding config (settings.json/.codex/config.toml). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, suspend the account's proxy/API credentials and isolate the host before the agent can iterate. 3) Hunt: correlate with newcli.com egress and DeepSeek/dashscope API traffic from the same host to confirm an autonomous offensive agent rather than benign dev use.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER","CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC","dangerously-skip-permissions","disable_response_storage")
      or (ProcessCommandLine has "approvalMode" and ProcessCommandLine has "yolo")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER","CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC","dangerously-skip-permissions","disable_response_storage")
      or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "approvalMode" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "yolo")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hermes Agent autonomous FOFA + Langflow PoC scanner execution AIReconnaissance High
Hunts execution of the actor's custom autonomous-enumeration scripts: fofoapi.py (FOFA cyberspace search), the FofaMap-Platinum-Full-Expert MCP server, and langflow_poc.py run with --scan-file langflow_targets.txt --threads 10. These are the concrete tooling artifacts of the DeepSeek/Hermes Agent recon-and-exploit loop. Rationale: langflow_poc.py --scan-file langflow_targets.txt --threads 10, fofoapi.py and FofaMap-Platinum-Full-Expert are quoted directly from the Phase-1 Langflow narrative and Hermes Agent skill list; these filenames are attacker-unique and not present in any benign toolchain. Cross-checked against: • https://securityaffairs.com/196544/ai/ai-runs-the-hack-chinese-actor-automates-cyberattacks-with-deepseek.html
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Blue-team member re-running the public langflow_poc.py to validate internal patch status
  • Security researcher analyzing the recovered toolkit on a lab host
  • A defensive FOFA/attack-surface script that happens to reuse the fofoapi.py filename
  • Purple-team exercise replaying the Hermes Agent chain under authorization
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\BlueTeam\\" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line, parent process (python/agent runtime), and the contents of langflow_targets.txt to scope which of your assets were enumerated. 2) Contain: isolate the executing host, revoke any FOFA/API keys found in fofoapi.py, and block outbound scanning at the egress firewall. 3) Hunt: cross-reference the target list against inbound Langflow exploitation logs (see the CVE-2026-33017 endpoint UC) and check for newcli.com / DeepSeek egress from the same host.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

Direct egress to DeepSeek / Qwen (dashscope) LLM APIs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts hosts reaching api.deepseek.com and dashscope.aliyuncs.com, the native endpoints this actor called directly (bypassing the newcli proxy) to drive DeepSeek and the Qwen/GLM/Kimi/MiniMax reasoning models. Flags AI-inference egress from servers or non-developer systems where it should not occur. Rationale: api.deepseek.com and dashscope.aliyuncs.com are the exact 'Direct API' access methods in Table 1; scoping to servers/non-dev hosts (not the raw domain) makes this a strong indicator of an autonomous offensive agent's reasoning-model callbacks. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-uses-deepseek-ai-to-autonomously-attack-vulnerable-servers/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chinese-hacker-commands-deepseek-via.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer or data-science team evaluating DeepSeek/Qwen models on a sanctioned workstation
  • Application backend that integrates dashscope for a production AI feature
  • Browser telemetry from an employee reading DeepSeek's website
  • Third-party SaaS agent on the host that legitimately calls these inference APIs
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["approved-ai-dev-01","approved-ai-dev-02"])) and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine host role (server/DC vs. sanctioned AI-dev laptop) and the initiating process; inference egress from a server or service account is the anomaly, not the domain itself. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, block the domains at egress and isolate the host pending review of the calling process. 3) Hunt: pivot the same host to newcli.com egress, the anti-attribution config UC, and the FOFA/Langflow scanner UC to confirm a full autonomous-agent footprint.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.deepseek.com","dashscope.aliyuncs.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Cmds=make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 5) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("api.deepseek.com","dashscope.aliyuncs.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Lookups=count() by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

Langflow CVE-2026-33017 unauth RCE endpoint exploitation (inbound) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the vulnerable Langflow endpoint /api/v1/build_public_tmp/ that this actor's langflow_poc.py targeted (CVE-2026-33017, CVSS 9.8, exec()-based unauth RCE). Surfaces attempts against your own Langflow 1.x instances regardless of source. Rationale: The vulnerable path /api/v1/build_public_tmp/{flow_id}/flow is the confirmed CVE-2026-33017 sink (JFrog/Orca/CSA, CISA KEV) that the article's langflow_poc.py scanner drives; the URI substring is attacker-unique to this exploit and cheap to match in web logs. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/langflow-latest-version-was-not-fixed/ • https://orca.security/resources/blog/langflow-rce-vulnerability-cve-2026-33017/ • https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-cve-2026-33017-langflow-ai-pipeline-rce-20/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow public-share feature invoked by authorized internal users
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) authorized to probe the same endpoint
  • Blue-team validation of patch status against the recovered PoC
  • Load balancer or uptime monitor hitting the flow endpoint as a health check
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.0") and csUserAgent !has "Nessus" and csUserAgent !has "Qualys"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check scStatus/response codes and csUriQuery for injected Python/data field payloads; a 200 on a POST to build_public_tmp from an external IP is likely a hit. 2) Contain: confirm the Langflow version, upgrade to >=1.9.0 (note JFrog found earlier 'fixed' builds still exploitable), and firewall the endpoint; snapshot the host for the exec() child-process forensics. 3) Hunt: on the Langflow host, hunt for python spawning shell/curl children and outbound connections initiated shortly after the request; cross-check source IPs against the actor's FOFA-enumerated target list.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp/"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Langflow CVE-2026-33017 Public Flow Build RCE Endpoint Access
id: 9d3a6f18-2b74-4e51-8c9b-0f5a7c2e14d6
description: Detects inbound requests to Langflow's /api/v1/build_public_tmp/ endpoint, the unauthenticated exec() code-injection path (CVE-2026-33017) probed by the DeepSeek/Hermes Agent operator's langflow_poc.py.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
  - https://research.jfrog.com/post/langflow-latest-version-was-not-fixed/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-method: 'POST'
    c-uri|contains: '/api/v1/build_public_tmp/'
  condition: selection
level: high
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/v1/build_public_tmp/*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.url Web.status Web.http_user_agent
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/v1/build_public_tmp/*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.url Web.status Web.http_user_agent
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("code.newcli.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["code.newcli.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("code.newcli.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("code.newcli.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("code.newcli.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("code.newcli.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] External-partner VPN logon with valid credentials (trusted-relationship abuse)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Toy Ghouls’ new toy: the GenieLocker ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] socks5.exe / anomalous Windows OpenSSH server for pivot tunneling · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Reverse SSH tunnel and C2 beacon to GenieLocker C2 89.125.66.101 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GenieLocker Windows ransomware execution via secret-argument hex + --percent/--recursive flags · [LLM] Mimikatz credential dumping via command-line/module signature · [LLM] KeePassXC .kdbx vault access/copy by non-KeePass process · [LLM] GenieLocker ELF encryptor on Linux/ESXi via --percent/--recursive flags · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change
GenieLocker Windows ransomware execution via secret-argument hex + --percent/--recursive flags AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts execution of the GenieLocker PE encryptor, which requires a long hex 'secret argument' as its first parameter and exposes distinctive --percent/-p and --recursive/-r CLI flags plus a -l/--log path. Anchors on the confirmed Windows sample MD5 and the malware's unique command-line shape. Rationale: Uses the article's confirmed Windows sample MD5 (5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c) and the malware's documented argument table (-p/--percent, -r/--recursive, -l/--log) — the --percent+--recursive combination is a rare, high-fidelity anchor for an encryptor. Cross-checked with gbhackers and mallory.ai malware profiles. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://gbhackers.com/new-genielocker-ransomware-encrypts-windows-linux-and-vmware-esxi-systems/ • https://mallory.ai/malware/019d2af9-67da-7113-b5e6-2e6c809b97b1
ATT&CKT1486 T1480.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backup/imaging utility invoked with both --percent (progress) and --recursive flags
  • Custom sysadmin file-processing scripts that mirror those long-flag names
  • Security-team detonation of the sample in a sandbox using the real secret argument
  • File-integrity or compression tools with a --recursive + --log combination
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.manager.exe","veeamagent.exe") and MD5 != "5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent process; confirm the first argument is a long hex string and MD5 matches a GenieLocker sample. Check the target path passed as the last argument. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network immediately, kill the process tree, and preserve volatile memory before shutdown to avoid losing per-file keys. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same MD5 and the --percent/--recursive command line across all hosts (mass deployment via PsExec/PAExec is expected), and look for preceding netscan.exe/mimikatz/socks5.exe activity on the same account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where MD5 == "5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--log")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "--percent" and CommandLine has "--recursive") or (CommandLine has "--percent" and CommandLine has "--log")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GenieLocker Windows Ransomware Execution (secret-arg + encrypt flags)
id: 7c3a1e42-9f1b-4c67-b0e2-1a4d9b2c8e10
description: Detects GenieLocker PE encryptor via its confirmed MD5 or its distinctive --percent/--recursive/--log command-line flags.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

tags:

logsource:

detection:

falsepositives:
  - Legitimate archivers or backup CLIs that coincidentally use --percent and --recursive together
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Hashes:*5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c* OR (@CommandLine:*--percent* AND @CommandLine:*--recursive*) OR (@CommandLine:*--percent* AND @CommandLine:*--log*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| MD5HashData=/^5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c$/i OR (regex("--percent", field=CommandLine) AND regex("--recursive", field=CommandLine)) OR (regex("--percent", field=CommandLine) AND regex("--log", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, MD5HashData], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_hash="5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c" OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--recursive*") OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--log*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
External-partner VPN logon with valid credentials (trusted-relationship abuse) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the GenieLocker initial-access vector: successful network/RDP logons using valid domain credentials that originate from a public (external partner) IP, consistent with the reported OpenVPN entry from a trusted partner's network. Flags externally-sourced authenticated sessions that precede internal tooling activity. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit initial-access statement (OpenVPN from an external partner network with stolen-but-valid credentials, T1199 trusted relationship). Detects authenticated sessions sourced from public IPs — the observable signature of externally-terminated VPN/RDP access with valid accounts. Confirmed by cybersecuritynews and gbhackers write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/genielocker-ransomware-attack/
ATT&CKT1078 T1199
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate partner/vendor remote support sessions over VPN or RDP
  • Remote employees connecting from home ISPs when the VPN gateway forwards the real public source IP
  • Cloud-hosted jump boxes with public NICs authenticating to domain resources
  • Split-tunnel VPN configurations that expose the client's public IP on network logons
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("<approved-partner-vpn-egress-not-applicable>") == false
Response runbook
1) Triage: geolocate the RemoteIP and confirm whether it belongs to a sanctioned partner range; verify the account is expected to authenticate externally and whether MFA was satisfied. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, disable the account, force credential reset, and terminate active sessions at the VPN concentrator. 3) Hunt: pivot on the account across DeviceProcessEvents for netscan.exe/mimikatz/socks5.exe and on DeviceLogonEvents for subsequent RDP/SSH lateral movement to other hosts.
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where LogonType in ("Network","RemoteInteractive")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hosts=make_set(DeviceName,20), Count=count() by AccountName, RemoteIP, LogonType
| order by FirstSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4624
| where LogonType in (3,10)
| where isnotempty(IpAddress) and IpAddress !in ("-","::1","127.0.0.1")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(IpAddress))
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Hosts=make_set(Computer,20) by TargetUserName, IpAddress, LogonType
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4624 @LogonType:(3 OR 10) NOT (CIDR(@IpAddress, 10.0.0.0/8) OR CIDR(@IpAddress, 172.16.0.0/12) OR CIDR(@IpAddress, 192.168.0.0/16)) -@TargetUserName:*$
#event_simpleName=UserLogon
| LogonType=/^(3|10)$/
| RemoteAddressIP4=*
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| UserName!=/\$$/
| groupBy([UserName, RemoteAddressIP4, LogonType, ComputerName], function=count())
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="success" (Authentication.authentication_method="NTLM" OR Authentication.authentication_method="Kerberos" OR nodename=Authentication) by Authentication.src Authentication.user Authentication.dest Authentication.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where user!="*$" AND NOT (cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src)) | iplocation src | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="success" (Authentication.authentication_method="NTLM" OR Authentication.authentication_method="Kerberos" OR nodename=Authentication) by Authentication.src Authentication.user Authentication.dest Authentication.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where user!="*$" AND NOT (cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src)) | iplocation src | sort - lastTime
SoftPerfect Network Scanner (netscan.exe) execution for internal discovery AIReconnaissance High
Detects the SoftPerfect Network Scanner used by Toy Ghouls for host/network discovery, matching on the netscan.exe image name and, resiliently, on the SoftPerfect vendor/product version metadata so renamed copies are still caught. Rationale: Article names 'SoftPerfect Network Scanner' as the discovery tool. Anchoring on both the netscan.exe image name and the SoftPerfect product/company PE metadata defeats simple renames while staying specific to this campaign's toolset. Corroborated by gbhackers and cybersecuritynews. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://gbhackers.com/new-genielocker-ransomware-encrypts-windows-linux-and-vmware-esxi-systems/
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned IT teams using SoftPerfect Network Scanner for asset inventory
  • Network engineers troubleshooting connectivity with the same tool
  • MSP/consultant onboarding scans
  • Vulnerability-management pilots evaluating SoftPerfect
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-itasset","svc-netmon")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the executing account and host are authorized to run network-scanning tools; review the scan's target ranges in the command line/config. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the host and disable the account pending review. 3) Hunt: on the same host/account look for Mimikatz command lines, socks5.exe/sshd.exe, and outbound connections to 89.125.66.101 — netscan is typically the discovery step that precedes credential access and lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "netscan.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "netscan.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Network Scanner"
   or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "SoftPerfect"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\netscan.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
