Mimikatz credential dumping via command-line/module signature AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Mimikatz execution used by Toy Ghouls to dump credentials, anchoring on its signature command modules (sekurlsa::, lsadump::, privilege::debug) and PE metadata rather than LSASS memory access, so renamed binaries are still caught. Rationale: Article states Mimikatz was used to dump credentials. Matching on module strings (sekurlsa::/lsadump::/privilege::debug) and gentilkiwi PE metadata is high-fidelity and deliberately avoids the pre-existing generic LSASS-access rule. Corroborated by cybersecuritynews and gbhackers. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/genielocker-ransomware-attack/
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned red-team/pentest engagements running Mimikatz
  • Security tooling that bundles Mimikatz modules for detection testing
  • EDR/AV signature files containing the module strings scanned into a command line (rare)
  • Purple-team detection-validation exercises
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "redteam" and DeviceName !in~ ("PURPLELAB01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and parent process; confirm elevation (privilege::debug requires admin) and whether an active red-team engagement is scheduled. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-reset credentials for every account that had a session on it, and rotate service-account/krbtgt if domain admin material was exposed. 3) Hunt: pivot on the harvested accounts across DeviceLogonEvents for RDP/SSH lateral movement and on KeePassXC .kdbx access on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sekurlsa::","lsadump::","privilege::debug","kerberos::","crypto::","mimikatz")
   or FileName =~ "mimikatz.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "mimikatz.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoFileDescription has "mimikatz"
   or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "gentilkiwi"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("sekurlsa::","lsadump::","privilege::debug","kerberos::","mimikatz")
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\mimikatz.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

KeePassXC .kdbx vault access/copy by non-KeePass process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects attempts to steal credentials from KeePassXC databases, as reported in the intrusion: a .kdbx file being created/copied or referenced in a command line by any process other than KeePassXC/KeePass (shells, archivers, copy utilities). Rationale: Article states the actors accessed KeePassXC databases on several hosts to extract stored credentials. A .kdbx write/copy by anything other than the KeePass client is a targeted, high-signal credential-store theft indicator (T1555.005). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/
ATT&CKT1555.005 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup agents (Veeam, CrashPlan, OneDrive/Backup) copying profile folders containing .kdbx
  • A user manually copying their own vault to a USB drive or network share
  • File-sync clients (Dropbox/Nextcloud) replicating a .kdbx
  • Migration tooling moving a user profile to a new machine
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeamagent.exe","onedrive.exe","dropbox.exe","backup.exe") and FolderPath !has "\\Backup\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and destination path — a copy to Temp/Public/network share or an archiver (7z/rar) reading .kdbx is high concern; a backup agent to a backup path is likely benign. 2) Contain: if malicious, isolate the host and force reset of every credential potentially stored in that vault. 3) Hunt: correlate with Mimikatz execution and outbound transfer/staging on the same host, and check whether the .kdbx was subsequently archived or moved toward the C2 IP 89.125.66.101.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".kdbx"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("keepassxc.exe","keepass.exe","keepassxc-cli.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, PreviousFolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".kdbx"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName !has "keepass"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: KeePassXC .kdbx Vault Copy by Non-KeePass Process

socks5.exe / anomalous Windows OpenSSH server for pivot tunneling AIInstallation Medium
Detects the pivot/tunneling toolkit Toy Ghouls installed on compromised Windows hosts — the named socks5.exe proxy binary, an OpenSSH sshd.exe server running on a Windows endpoint, and ssh.exe dynamic-SOCKS (-D) proxying — used to build lateral-movement infrastructure. Rationale: Article lists socks5.exe and OpenSSH among tools installed on compromised hosts for pivoting. socks5.exe is a specific binary name; an sshd.exe server or ssh -D dynamic proxy on Windows endpoints is anomalous tunneling infrastructure (T1572/T1090). Confirmed by gbhackers. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://gbhackers.com/new-genielocker-ransomware-encrypts-windows-linux-and-vmware-esxi-systems/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1021.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Servers where Windows OpenSSH Server (sshd.exe) is a sanctioned, installed role
  • Developers/admins using ssh -D for legitimate SOCKS forwarding
  • Third-party VPN or remote-access software that bundles a socks proxy component
  • Automation/CI agents launching sshd for build tasks
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "sshd.exe" and DeviceName in~ ("LINUXJUMP01","SSHGW01"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether OpenSSH Server / SOCKS proxying is an approved service on this host; review the binary path (Temp/Public/user profile = suspicious) and command-line listen ports. 2) Contain: kill the process, block the listening port, and isolate the host if the tooling is unsanctioned. 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents from this host to 89.125.66.101 and for inbound connections to the socks/ssh listener from other internal hosts (pivot fan-out).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "socks5.exe"
   or FileName =~ "sshd.exe"
   or (FileName =~ "ssh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-D")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\socks5.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\sshd.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\\ssh.exe" and CommandLine has "-D")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: socks5.exe / Anomalous OpenSSH Server on Windows (Toy Ghouls pivot)
id: 5f2b8c91-7a63-4d0e-b1a4-9c3e2d6f8b17
description: Detects socks5.exe proxy, a Windows OpenSSH sshd server, or ssh.exe dynamic-SOCKS proxying used for lateral-movement tunneling.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:

  - attack.t1090
  - attack.t1021.004
logsource:

detection:

  selection_sshd:

  selection_dynproxy:

  condition: selection_socks or selection_sshd or selection_dynproxy
falsepositives:
  - Servers where OpenSSH Server is an approved role
  - Developers using ssh -D for legitimate SOCKS forwarding
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\socks5.exe OR *\\SOCKS5.exe) OR @Image:(*\\sshd.exe OR *\\SSHD.exe) OR (@Image:(*\\ssh.exe OR *\\SSH.exe) AND @CommandLine:*\ -D\ *))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\socks5\.exe$/i OR ImageFileName=/\\sshd\.exe$/i OR (ImageFileName=/\\ssh\.exe$/i AND regex("\\s-D\\s", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="socks5.exe" OR Processes.process_name="sshd.exe" OR (Processes.process_name="ssh.exe" AND Processes.process="*-D *")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="socks5.exe" OR Processes.process_name="sshd.exe" OR (Processes.process_name="ssh.exe" AND Processes.process="*-D *")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Reverse SSH tunnel and C2 beacon to GenieLocker C2 89.125.66.101 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the reverse SSH tunnel Toy Ghouls established for command-and-control: any outbound connection to the confirmed C2 IP 89.125.66.101, and ssh.exe/plink reverse-forwarding (-R) to a public host — the network signature of the C2 channel. Rationale: IP 89.125.66.101 is the article's C2 indicator (corroborated by the Securelist IOC list and mallory.ai). Combined with ssh.exe/plink '-R' reverse-forwarding to public destinations — the exact reverse-SSH-tunnel C2 technique the article describes — this is a high-fidelity C2 detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://mallory.ai/malware/019d2af9-67da-7113-b5e6-2e6c809b97b1
ATT&CKT1572 T1071 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/allowlist scanners or sinkholes deliberately touching the IOC
  • Security researchers detonating samples in a monitored lab
  • Admins using ssh -R for legitimate reverse-forwarding to a sanctioned bastion
  • Netflow re-ingestion causing historical hits after the IOC is already remediated
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "threatintel" and DeviceName !in~ ("MALWARELAB01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (ContextImageFileName/InitiatingProcessFileName) and account driving the connection to 89.125.66.101; determine direction and byte volume. 2) Contain: block 89.125.66.101 at the perimeter, isolate the beaconing host, and terminate any ssh.exe/plink -R sessions. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for connections to the IP and for socks5.exe/sshd.exe pivot infrastructure, then check for GenieLocker execution (UC1) as encryption often follows C2 setup.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "89.125.66.101"
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ssh.exe","plink.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-R" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "89.125.66.101"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound Connection to GenieLocker C2 89.125.66.101
id: 2c7d9e14-3f60-4a81-9b52-6e1a4c8d0f39
description: Detects any outbound network connection to the confirmed GenieLocker command-and-control IP.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:

detection:
  selection:
    DestinationIp: '89.125.66.101'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Threat-intel scanning or sinkhole infrastructure legitimately probing the IP
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:89.125.66.101) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\ssh.exe OR *\\SSH.exe OR *\\plink.exe) @CommandLine:*\ -R\ *)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| RemoteAddressIP4=/^89\.125\.66\.101$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="89.125.66.101" by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime

GenieLocker ELF encryptor on Linux/ESXi via --percent/--recursive flags AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GenieLocker ELF build used to encrypt Linux servers and ESXi datastores after stopping running VMs. Anchors on the shared encryptor CLI flags (--percent/-p, --recursive/-r, --log/-l) executed on Linux hosts. Rationale: Article documents an ELF GenieLocker build encrypting Linux/ESXi servers after stopping VMs, sharing the same argument set (-p/--percent, -r/--recursive, -l/--log) as the Windows build. Scoping those flags to Linux process telemetry targets the ESXi/Linux impact phase. Cross-platform behaviour confirmed by technadu and gbhackers. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://www.technadu.com/genielocker-ransomware-targets-windows-linux-and-esxi-systems-leaves-no-ransom-note/632252/
ATT&CKT1486 T1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Linux backup or rsync-style utilities invoked with --percent progress and --recursive together
  • ESXi/admin maintenance scripts that batch-process datastore files with similar flags
  • Media/transcoding jobs using --recursive over a tree with a --log destination
  • Legitimate encryption/compression CLI tools run by admins
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("rsync","tar","borg","restic","duplicity")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the path argument; on ESXi correlate with recent vmsvc power-off / VM shutdown activity and check the binary against GenieLocker ELF hashes. 2) Contain: kill the process, disconnect the host/datastore from the network, and protect backups/snapshots from deletion. 3) Hunt: check SSH access logs for the reverse tunnel and connections to 89.125.66.101, and review other Linux/ESXi hosts reachable over SSH for the same flag pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--log")
| where FolderPath startswith "/" or FolderPath has "/tmp/" or FolderPath has "/var/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DvcOs has "Linux" or ActingProcessName startswith "/"
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
     or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--log")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GenieLocker ELF Encryptor Execution on Linux/ESXi
id: 8b1e4d02-5c39-47a6-9e70-3d2f6a1c9b84

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 event_platform=Lin

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--recursive*") OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--log*")) AND Processes.os="Linux" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteIP in ("89.125.66.101") or RemoteUrl has_any ("")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["89.125.66.101"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic([""]);
ImNetworkSession

   or Url has_any (BadDomains)

      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental

    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.

        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender

Command & Control. OWAReaper server-side persistence: Owner rights granted to Default/Anonymous on mail folders AIInstallation High
Hunts the core OWAReaper persistence mechanism where the implant uses Outlook APIs to grant Owner-level permissions to the Default (or Anonymous) principal on every mail folder, giving any authenticated org user complete mailbox access that survives credential rotation and device re-imaging. Fires on Add/Set-MailboxFolderPermission cmdlets assigning Owner/Editor rights to Default or Anonymous. Rationale: Article states OWAReaper 'grants itself Owner-level permissions to the Default user on every mail folder... grants complete mailbox access to any authenticated user' and that this 'lives on the server-side and requires deliberate removal from the Exchange server.' Granting Owner/Editor to Default/Anonymous is the highest-fidelity, article-specific persistence artifact and is directly logged in Exchange admin audit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-exploit-exchange-owa-zero-day-for-long-term-mailbox-access/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/30/cve-2026-42897-microsoft-exchange-email-attack/
ATT&CKT1098.002 T1098
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Calendar-sharing/publishing that sets Default to Reviewer or AvailabilityOnly (not Owner) — excluded by the rights filter
  • Shared/resource mailbox admin delegation scripts intentionally opening a mailbox to Default
  • Mailbox migration or coexistence tooling re-applying folder permissions in bulk
  • Help-desk delegation runbooks granting Editor on a specific folder to a named team member (User is not Default/Anonymous)
Suppression filter
| where not (Parameters has_any ("AvailabilityOnly","LimitedDetails","Reviewer","None") and Parameters !has "Owner" and Parameters !has "Editor")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full Parameters/RawEventData — confirm the User is literally 'Default' or 'Anonymous' and AccessRights includes Owner/Editor; identify the acting principal (UserId/AccountId) and ClientIP, and whether the acting account is itself recently compromised. 2) Contain: run Remove-MailboxFolderPermission to strip Default/Anonymous Owner rights on every folder of the affected mailbox, revoke the acting account's sessions/tokens (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken), and force MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: enumerate all mailboxes in the org for Default/Anonymous Owner/Editor grants, review the acting IP for connections to asecdns.com/acocdn.com/dnsrecursive.eu/tdndns.com, and check for OWAReaper's localStorage/IndexedDB re-infection on the victim's browser.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application has "Exchange"
| where ActionType in~ ("Add-MailboxFolderPermission","Set-MailboxFolderPermission")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("Owner","Editor","PublishingEditor")
| where Raw has_any ("Default","Anonymous")
| project Timestamp, ActingUser = AccountDisplayName, AccountId, IPAddress, ActionType, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Operation in~ ("Add-MailboxFolderPermission","Set-MailboxFolderPermission")
| where Parameters has_any ("Owner","Editor","PublishingEditor")
| where Parameters has_any ("Default","Anonymous")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, MailboxOwnerUPN, Parameters, ResultStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OWAReaper C2 / exfiltration to TA488-controlled domains (HTTPS + DNS label tunneling) AICommand & Control High
Detects any host resolving or connecting to the four attacker-controlled OWAReaper domains used for HTTPS exfiltration and DNS-label tunneling. High-fidelity IOC match confirmed by multiple second sources; matches parent domain to also catch DNS-tunnel subdomains. Rationale: asecdns.com, acocdn.com, dnsrecursive.eu and tdndns.com are the pre-extracted C2/exfil domains and were independently confirmed by BleepingComputer and betanews; the article states exfil is 'primarily over HTTPS with AES-CTR encrypted URI paths' with fallback to 'DNS label tunneling... of an actor-controlled domain', so both endswith (subdomain-tunnel) and URL matches apply. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-exploit-exchange-owa-zero-day-for-long-term-mailbox-access/ • https://betanews.com/article/russian-hackers-owareaper-exchange-backdoor/ • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1572 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanners / sandboxes in the org deliberately resolving these IOCs for enrichment
  • Security researcher workstation reproducing the campaign
  • Passive DNS or DNS-sinkhole appliance logging the domains as it blocks them
  • Typo-squat collisions are unlikely given the specific TLDs but a benign lookalike could theoretically appear
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host, the ContextImageFileName/InitiatingProcess (expect a browser process hosting the OWA tab), and whether the query is a bare apex or a long random subdomain label (DNS tunnel). 2) Contain: block all four domains at the resolver/proxy, isolate the host's browser session, and clear OWAReaper's browser localStorage/IndexedDB persistence for the user. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolving browser process for concurrent HTTPS beacons routed through image CDNs (images.weserv.nl, i3.wp.com, slack-imgs.com) toward acocdn.com, and check the user's mailbox for Default/Anonymous Owner folder-permission grants.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("asecdns.com","acocdn.com","dnsrecursive.eu","tdndns.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("asecdns.com","acocdn.com","dnsrecursive.eu","tdndns.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Successful OWA/Exchange access within 24h of a password reset (post-rotation mailbox access) AIInstallation Medium
Correlates an Azure AD password reset/change with a subsequent successful sign-in to Office 365 Exchange Online for the same user within 24 hours — the exact 'access survives credential rotation' thesis of the OWAReaper campaign. Surfaces access that should have been invalidated by the reset. Rationale: Directly targets the article's headline claim that 'credential rotation... will not evict the actor' — a successful Exchange Online sign-in inside a 24h window after a password reset for the same UPN is the observable signature of persistence that ignored the rotation. Correlation of AuditLogs reset + SigninLogs success on the Exchange resource keeps it specific. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-exploit-exchange-owa-zero-day-for-long-term-mailbox-access/
ATT&CKT1098.002 T1550
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user resets their own password then immediately signs back into webmail (most common benign case)
  • Help-desk resets a password and the user logs in the same day from a known device/location
  • Session that re-authenticates with a fresh MFA challenge after reset (add MFA filter to suppress)
  • Password-expiry-driven change during an active OWA session on a managed corporate IP
Suppression filter
| where AuthenticationRequirement != "multiFactorAuthentication"
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the post-reset sign-in IP/geo/device and AuthenticationRequirement against the user's baseline — a single-factor success from an unfamiliar IP is the alarm; a compliant device from a normal location is likely benign. 2) Contain: if suspicious, revoke all refresh tokens (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken), re-reset the password, enforce MFA re-registration, and audit the mailbox for Default/Anonymous folder permissions (server-side persistence the reset can't clear). 3) Hunt: check the source IP for the four OWAReaper C2 domains and for other org accounts signing into the same victim mailbox (delegate access granted by OWAReaper).
let resets = IdentityDirectoryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("Account Password changed","Account Password reset")
| project ResetTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ResourceDisplayName == "Office 365 Exchange Online"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where Application has_any ("Outlook","OWA","Exchange")
| join kind=inner resets on AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + 24h)
| extend MinutesAfterReset = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, ResetTime)
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, ResetTime, MinutesAfterReset, IPAddress, Country, ClientAppUsed, Application, AuthenticationRequirement
| order by Timestamp desc
let resets = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName in ("Reset user password","Change user password","Reset password (self-service)")
| extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| where isnotempty(TargetUpn)
| project ResetTime = TimeGenerated, TargetUpn;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResourceDisplayName == "Office 365 Exchange Online"
| where ResultType == 0
| where AppDisplayName has_any ("Outlook","OWA","Exchange")
| join kind=inner resets on $left.UserPrincipalName == $right.TargetUpn
| where TimeGenerated between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + 24h)
| extend MinutesAfterReset = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, ResetTime)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, ResetTime, MinutesAfterReset, IPAddress, Location, ClientAppUsed, AppDisplayName, AuthenticationRequirement
| order by TimeGenerated desc
First-seen OWA/Exchange sign-in from Russian IP space for a user with no RU history AICommand & Control Medium
Baselines each user's Exchange Online sign-in geography over 30 days and alerts on a first-time successful sign-in from Russian IP space, aligned to TA488/Void Blizzard attribution. Anti-join against prior RU activity keeps it low-noise versus a blanket geo block. Rationale: The campaign is attributed to Russia-aligned TA488/Void Blizzard; scoping to first-ever successful RU sign-ins against the Exchange Online resource (leftanti a 60-day RU baseline) turns a broad geo signal into a per-user first-seen anomaly on the exact resource OWAReaper abuses. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/ta488-outlook-half-click-owareaper/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1071.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee traveling to Russia signing into webmail for the first time
  • VPN/anycast egress that geolocates to RU incorrectly
  • New hire whose first-ever sign-in happens to originate from RU (no baseline exists to compare)
  • Roaming mobile carrier that presents a Russian ASN
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the IP/ASN is genuinely Russian hosting (not a VPN/travel), and check whether the same UPN also has a recent password reset or Default-Owner folder grant. 2) Contain: if unexplained, revoke tokens, reset the password, and apply a Conditional Access block for the user; preserve the sign-in session details. 3) Hunt: sweep the RU source IP/ASN for other org users, correlate with resolutions to the four OWAReaper C2 domains, and audit mailbox folder permissions across affected users.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4") or SHA1 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4") or MD5 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4") or SHA1 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4") or MD5 in~ ("6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6897b649f29e54d8910459963bbf94ed5c7a4fe66a56bc5962540b226b8e48c4"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

High

Amazon Links Debug and Chalk npm Hijack to North Korea’s Sapphire Sleet

The Hacker News
2026-07-30 13 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Amazon has tied the September 2025 hijack of the npm packages debug and chalk to North Korea. For ten months, the incident sat in the public record as crypto theft: a maintainer phished through a lookalike npm domain and a wallet-draining script pushed into at least 18 packages carrying more than 2 billion weekly downloads between them. The original Aikido and Wiz reports did not attribute the

IPs216.74.123.126
SHA25624604384b0e748ad… 2014d09c7ded74d8…

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] npm registry look-alike phishing domains (npmjs.help / npmjs.store) in mail & web · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Amazon Links Debug and Chalk npm Hijack to North Korea’s Sapphire Sleet
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Known Sapphire Sleet npm payload hashes written or executed · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Sapphire Sleet npm supply-chain C2 egress to npmjs.store / 216.74.123.126 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Sapphire Sleet npm supply-chain C2 egress to npmjs.store / 216.74.123.126 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to the DPRK-attributed npm supply-chain C2 (domain npmjs.store, IP 216.74.123.126) tied to the trojanized debug/chalk/axios/typo-crypto packages. npmjs.store is a registry look-alike that is never a legitimate npm endpoint (real registry is registry.npmjs.org / npmjs.com), so a hit is a high-fidelity compromise signal on a developer or CI/CD host. Rationale: Uses the two network IOCs Amazon published (domain npmjs.store, IP 216.74.123.126). npmjs.store is a registry look-alike with no legitimate use, giving near-zero baseline noise. Cross-checked BleepingComputer, The Hacker News and the AWS Security blog which all list the same infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/amazon-identifies-north-korean-hacker-group-behind-open-source-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/amazon-links-debug-chalk-npm-supply-chain-attacks-to-north-korean-hackers/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/amazon-links-debug-and-chalk-npm-hijack.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or CI sandbox detonating a compromised package sample and resolving the C2 on purpose
  • Threat-intel enrichment/crawler tooling (e.g. urlscan agents) resolving npmjs.store from a SOC egress host
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS appliance logging the query as it blackholes it
  • IP 216.74.123.126 later reassigned by its shared-hosting provider to a benign tenant, generating stale-IOC hits
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe", "SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 Triage: identify the process that made the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine) — expect node.exe, npm, a build agent, or a browser; confirm whether the host recently ran `npm install` / has debug/chalk/axios in a lockfile. Step 2 Contain: isolate the host, block npmjs.store + 216.74.123.126 at proxy/firewall/protective-DNS, and rotate any crypto-wallet keys, npm tokens and cloud credentials that touched the machine. Step 3 Hunt: pull package-lock.json/yarn.lock across the fleet for compromised versions, sweep all endpoints for the two known SHA256 payloads, and review CI/CD build logs for the C2 during the Sep-2025 / Mar-2026 windows.
let c2domain = "npmjs.store";
let c2ip = "216.74.123.126";
union
 (DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has c2domain or RemoteIP == c2ip
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Src="NetworkConnect"),
 (DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | where RemoteUrl has c2domain or AdditionalFields has c2ip
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, Src="DnsQuery")
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2domain = "npmjs.store";
let c2ip = "216.74.123.126";
union isfuzzy=true
 (ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has c2domain | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery, Indicator=c2domain, Src="DNS"),
 (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr == c2ip or DstHostname has c2domain | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Indicator=iff(DstIpAddr==c2ip, c2ip, c2domain), Src="Network"),
 (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationHostName has c2domain or DestinationIP == c2ip or RequestURL has c2domain | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestURL, Indicator=c2domain, Src="Proxy")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DPRK npm Supply-Chain C2 Domain Resolution (npmjs.store)

description: Detects DNS resolution of npmjs.store, the C2 domain Amazon attributed to Sapphire Sleet for the debug/chalk/axios npm supply-chain compromises.

  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/amazon-links-debug-and-chalk-npm-hijack.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/31
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:

  selection:

  condition: selection

(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:*npmjs.store*) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationHostname:*npmjs.store* OR @DestinationIp:216.74.123.126))

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
| count > 0
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, action, bytes
| filter dstAddr = "216.74.123.126"
| stats count(*) as flows, sum(bytes) as totalBytes by srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, action
| sort totalBytes desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="npmjs.store" OR DNS.query="*.npmjs.store" OR DNS.answer="216.74.123.126") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="npmjs.store" OR DNS.query="*.npmjs.store" OR DNS.answer="216.74.123.126") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Known Sapphire Sleet npm payload hashes written or executed AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the two malicious SHA256 payloads Amazon tied to the trojanized npm packages, on either file-write or process-execution. A match means the second-stage payload from the debug/chalk/axios/typo-crypto compromise landed on an endpoint or build agent. Rationale: Uses the two exact SHA256 IOCs from Amazon's report (typo-crypto package hash + trojanized core.js hash) as file-write and execution pivots — hash matches are deterministic and effectively FP-free. Distinct log-source pivot (file/hash) from the network UC. Verified against the AWS Security blog IOC list. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/amazon-identifies-north-korean-hacker-group-behind-open-source-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/amazon-links-debug-chalk-npm-supply-chain-attacks-to-north-korean-hackers/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR quarantine or sample-submission tooling copying the payload into a vault path (still worth reviewing)
  • A malware-analysis or reverse-engineering VM where an analyst intentionally staged the sample
  • Backup/DLP indexer re-hashing a previously quarantined artifact
Response runbook
Step 1 Triage: confirm the hash hit is a live artifact vs. an EDR quarantine copy; capture the FolderPath and the writing/executing process. Step 2 Contain: isolate the host, kill and quarantine the file, and revoke npm tokens, SSH keys and crypto-wallet material accessible from it. Step 3 Hunt: enumerate every host that installed debug/chalk/axios/typo-crypto in the affected version windows, and pivot on the same devices for outbound npmjs.store / 216.74.123.126 traffic to scope C2 reach.

 (DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where SHA256 in (mal) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName, ActorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, User=InitiatingProcessAccountName),
 (DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where SHA256 in (mal) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType="ProcessExec", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName, ActorCmd=ProcessCommandLine, User=AccountName)
| order by Timestamp desc

npm registry look-alike phishing domains (npmjs.help / npmjs.store) in mail & web AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the maintainer-phishing look-alike domains used to hijack npm maintainer accounts (npmjs.help credential-harvest page, npmjs.store) arriving via email links or being browsed. Targets the initial-access step Amazon described as 'socially engineering package maintainers' — catching your own developers being lured with the same kit. Rationale: Combines the C2/registry look-alike npmjs.store (Amazon) with the corroborated maintainer-phishing domain npmjs.help documented by Aikido and Semgrep for the Sep-2025 debug/chalk hijack. Different pivot (email/URL-click/web, initial access) from the network and hash UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-debug-and-chalk-packages-compromised • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2025/chalk-debug-and-color-on-npm-compromised-in-new-supply-chain-attack/ • https://cycode.com/blog/npm-debug-chalk-supply-chain-attack-the-complete-guide/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-awareness or phishing-simulation platform seeding these domains in a test campaign
  • SOC analyst manually browsing the domain during threat research from a corporate egress
  • Brand-protection / takedown vendor probing the look-alike domain
  • Threat-intel feed pre-fetching the URL for enrichment
Response runbook
Step 1 Triage: identify the recipient/user and whether a click occurred (IsClickedThrough) and whether credentials were submitted; check if the user is a package maintainer or holds npm publish rights. Step 2 Contain: block npmjs.help + npmjs.store at mail gateway and proxy, force-reset the user's npm and SSO credentials, and revoke active npm publish tokens. Step 3 Hunt: search mail flow for the same sender/URL across the org, review recent npm publish events for maintainer accounts, and pivot any clicking host to the C2/hash UCs to confirm downstream compromise.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73") or SHA1 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73") or MD5 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73") or SHA1 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73") or MD5 in~ ("24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["24604384b0e748ada07923630b3d037489e696284a98c4409fb9b6763565571f", "2014d09c7ded74d89c885b5f11693865224116f1b25df9330e61fe528f419d73"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco FMC Zero-Day Actively Exploited, Static Credentials Could Expose Sensitive Data

The Hacker News
2026-07-30 9 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added a newly disclosed security flaw impacting Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) Software to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports of zero-day exploitation. The vulnerability, assigned CVE-2026-20316 (CVSS score: 5.3), could permit an unauthenticated, remote attacker to log

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Cisco FMC CVE-2026-20079 auth bypass: pre-auth CGI callServerFunc / csm_processes session abuse · [LLM] Cisco FMC static/built-in service account authentication (CVE-2026-20316) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Cisco FMC Zero-Day Actively Exploited, Static Credentials Could Expose Sensitive
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Cisco FMC RCE artifact: www user runs package_info.pl as root against /var/tmp/license.tmp
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Cisco FMC RCE artifact: www user runs package_info.pl as root against /var/tmp/license.tmp AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact Cisco-published indicator of compromise for CVE-2026-20079/CVE-2026-20316 exploitation on Secure Firewall Management Center: the web-server account (www) invoking sudo to run /usr/local/sf/bin/package_info.pl against the attacker-controllable file /var/tmp/license.tmp as root. Legitimate license processing never targets /var/tmp/license.tmp, making this a near-zero-FP post-exploitation signal. Rationale: Anchored on the exact IOC line Cisco tells customers to grep for ('cat /var/log/messages | grep license' -> package_info.pl /var/tmp/license.tmp), corroborated by VulnCheck which confirms /var/tmp/license.tmp is the arbitrary-file-write target in the RCE chain. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch are empty because FMC is a Linux appliance with no such agents; telemetry only reaches SIEM via Syslog. Cross-checked against: • https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/cisco-fmc-auth-bypass-cve-2026-20079 • https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/csa/cisco-sa-fmc-static-cred-BET3Cjh.html • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-20079/
ATT&CKT1190 T1068 T1548.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cisco TAC-guided troubleshooting where an engineer manually stages a license file (would rarely use the /var/tmp/license.tmp path)
  • Security team reproducing the Cisco IOC-check command during hunt (creates a benign grep hit, not an actual sudo execution)
  • Backup/restore tooling copying appliance state that replays old /var/log/messages content into the SIEM
  • Automated FMC health scripts invoking package_info.pl against the real license under /var/sf/, not /var/tmp/license.tmp
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "grep" and SyslogMessage !has "COMMAND=/bin/grep"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the log is a live sudo execution (USER=root, COMMAND=package_info.pl /var/tmp/license.tmp), not a benign grep of the IOC-check command; note the FMC hostname, appliance version, and timestamp. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the FMC management interface from untrusted networks, snapshot /var/tmp/ and /var/log/messages for forensics, then apply the branch hot fix (7.0.9.1 / 7.2.11.1 / 7.4.7.1 / 7.6.5.1 / 7.7.12.1 / 10.0.1.1) and rotate all admin/API credentials. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to httpd access logs for the CVE-2026-20079 CGI bypass requests (sajaxintf.cgi callServerFunc, csm_processes session), review any managed-firewall policy pushes since the event, and check for new local accounts or SSH keys.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "package_info.pl" and SyslogMessage has "/var/tmp/license.tmp"
| where SyslogMessage has "USER=root"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco FMC CVE-2026-20079 auth bypass: pre-auth CGI callServerFunc / csm_processes session abuse AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-20079 authentication-bypass request chain against Secure FMC's web interface: unauthenticated calls to sajaxintf.cgi with rs=callServerFunc invoking validateLicense/batchResults/upgradeReadinessCall, and info-disclosure requests to about.cgi / ApplianceInformation.cgi riding the built-in csm_processes machine session. These endpoint+parameter combinations are the documented exploit primitives, not normal admin browsing. Rationale: Uses the exact CGI endpoints, query parameter (rs=callServerFunc), abused functions (validateLicense/batchResults/upgradeReadinessCall) and the csm_processes machine-session identifier that VulnCheck and Horizon3 document as the CVE-2026-20079 bypass-to-RCE primitives - none of which appear in normal authenticated FMC UI traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/cisco-fmc-auth-bypass-cve-2026-20079 • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-20079/ • https://kudelskisecurity.com/research/cisco-secure-firewall-management-center-fmc-authentication-bypass-and-rce-vulnerabilities
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualls/Horizon3 NodeZero) probing the FMC with the public PoC
  • Cisco TAC or internal red team validating patch status against these CGIs
  • Legitimate license/smart-licensing sync traffic that also touches validateLicense but from an authenticated admin session
  • Post-patch appliances still logging historical exploit attempts replayed from archived syslog
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the source IP of the CGI requests and whether the FMC was rebooted recently (CVE-2026-20079 requires a persisted csm_processes session post-boot); confirm the appliance is on a pre-fix version. Step 2 (contain): Restrict the FMC management interface to trusted admin subnets, block the source IP at the perimeter, and apply the branch hot fix immediately (no workaround exists). Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with UC1 (www->root package_info.pl / /var/tmp/license.tmp) on the same host and timeframe to confirm bypass-to-RCE, then audit managed-firewall policy changes and new sessions in sfsnort.sessions.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (SyslogMessage has "sajaxintf.cgi" and SyslogMessage has "callServerFunc" and SyslogMessage has_any ("validateLicense","batchResults","upgradeReadinessCall"))
      or (SyslogMessage has_any ("/help/about.cgi","/platinum/ApplianceInformation.cgi") and SyslogMessage has "csm_processes")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
